extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, math researchers, and general readers interested in mathematics
extracted.subtask_short: assessing new proofs of known theorems
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and implicit standards for what makes a new proof of an old mathematical result interesting, valuable, or worth publishing — emphasizing novelty of method, insight, connections to other areas, pedagogy, and potential practical impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amusement and aesthetic value
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs may be undertaken for fun; the line between recreational math and serious math is thin. "It has to be amusing. Doing something technically awful is not the point. The only way you want to do something difficult is that it’s amusing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proof's technical difficulty is justified when it produces an amusing, elegant, or surprising perspective. Examples: competitive one-upmanship among mathematicians producing 'ridiculously difficult' proofs that are nevertheless entertaining or revealing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revealing hidden connections between areas
rubrics_metrics.description: A valuable new proof can 'reveal hidden connections between different areas of math' by bringing in techniques or theorems from distant fields to prove a familiar result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include using Fermat's Last Theorem, Schur's theorem, van der Waerden's theorem, Roth's theorem, or topology (Furstenberg) to reprove Euclid's theorem — each showing links between number theory, combinatorics, topology, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of novel or diverse methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is measured by the techniques used: proofs that draw on unexpected theorems or fields (analytic series, combinatorics, topology) are noteworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historic examples: Euler's analytic-series proof, Furstenberg's topological proof, combinatorial proofs using Schur or van der Waerden. Diversity of approach is itself a contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Producing new techniques or leading to substantive research
rubrics_metrics.description: A "cute new proof" is valuable when it 'segue[s] ... into serious math' — i.e., when it creates techniques or ways of thinking that lead to further results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good proofs often serve as seeds for further investigation (e.g., moving from a proof about primes to study 'densities of squares' or other deeper questions). Look for proofs that generate methods, not just an alternative argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical simplicity and classical elegance
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity and accessibility remain virtues: short, elementary proofs (like Euclid’s original proof) have pedagogical value and long-standing appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contrast between simple classical proofs and later sophisticated ones is important: a simple proof can be preferable for teaching, while sophisticated proofs may serve other aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification via contradiction and logical solidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Many reproofs proceed by assuming the negation (e.g., finitely many primes) and deriving a contradiction by invoking other theorems (Fermat, Euler, Roth, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should check that the chain of implications to contradiction is valid and that imported theorems are applied correctly (e.g., existence of colored configurations leading to impossible Diophantine equations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical or survey value
rubrics_metrics.description: Compilations and historical surveys that collect many proofs (e.g., Meštrović's ~200 proofs) are valuable for documenting the range of approaches and their contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such work is assessed by completeness, accuracy of historical attribution, clarity of exposition, and synthesis of themes across proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary or practical implications
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof gains additional interest if it suggests connections to practical problems or other disciplines (e.g., potential links to cryptography and hardness of factoring).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the new proof hints at implications outside pure theory (even 'weak connections' are noteworthy) and whether those implications are plausibly exploitable or suggest new research directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstration of surprising backward reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Using very deep theorems to prove elementary statements (working backward) can be informative: 'I use Fermat’s Last Theorem ... and then I conclude a very simple result.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such proofs should be evaluated for the insight they provide about dependencies of results rather than dismissed simply because they use heavy machinery for a simple conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sparsity and elegance of formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Concise, 'sparse elegance' in an argument is prized — a proof that employs minimal, clean ideas to reach a conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granville praised Furstenberg's 'sparse elegance'; evaluate whether the proof reduces clutter and highlights core mechanisms, not just complexity for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source diversity and accessibility of contributors
rubrics_metrics.description: New proofs can originate from varied contributors (students, postdocs, established researchers); this diversity is a positive sign for the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Furstenberg and Alpöge published while still in college. Evaluate how accessible the approach is to entrants and whether it fosters broader participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitive/priority dynamics vs. substantive contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a social dynamic ('a little competition ... for people to have the most ridiculously difficult proof'), but the community values substantive insight over mere technical one-upmanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a proof, distinguish between novelty-for-vanity (complexity without insight) and complexity that uncovers new mathematics or techniques.
